title: Conflict and safe relationships
outcome: Managing conflict & staying safe in relationships.
outcomes: Managing conflict & staying safe in relationships.
objectives: Tell a safe disagreement from pressure or control in a made-up story.
Explain a calm next step when both people feel safe and free to choose.
Choose adult help when a person feels afraid or cannot say no freely.
vocabulary: A disagreement about needs, ideas or choices.
A limit a person sets about what they will accept or do.
Treating a person's needs and choices as mattering.
Trying to take away another person's freedom to choose.
Help from a safe person, such as a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead.

model.title: Two safe choices
model.story: Two invented friends plan a display. One wants to draw. The other wants to write. Each can say no without fear. They pause, take turns to listen and agree to do one part each. Either can ask for more time or adult help.
model.reasoning: This is a safe disagreement. Each person has a voice and a real choice. Taking turns may help. An agreement works only if both choose it freely. If fear, pressure or control appears, stop the joint problem-solving task and get adult help.

cases.title: A change of plan
cases.story: Two invented friends plan a quiet game. One now wants to read. The other is disappointed but accepts a pause. Both can say no. Neither feels afraid.
questions: Which detail shows that each person still has a choice?
What calm step could help with this disagreement?
Why does neither person have to agree to a plan they do not want?
cases.answer: Both can say no, and a pause is accepted. They could listen in turn, explain the choice calmly or make separate plans. A shared plan needs free agreement. Disappointment alone does not remove the other person's choice. Adult support remains available.

cases.title: Rules for a friend
cases.story: In a made-up story, one friend keeps demanding to know where the other is. They say the other must stop talking to a different friend. The other person feels worried about saying no.
questions: Which details suggest pressure or control?
Should the worried person bargain about how much control is allowed?
What safer next step and adult help route could they choose?
cases.answer: Repeated demands for updates, rules about other friends and worry about saying no are warning signs. This is not a fair difference to split down the middle. The worried person is not to blame. They can stop the discussion, seek a safer place with adult support and tell a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead. They do not need to confront the friend or bargain away their choices.

cases.title: The first adult is busy
cases.story: An invented learner says a relationship leaves them afraid to say no. The first trusted adult is busy and cannot listen then. Another trusted member of staff and the safeguarding lead are available. The learner does not need to tell the whole class.
questions: Does the first adult being busy mean the learner must manage alone?
Who else could the learner tell, by role?
What could a private request for help say?
cases.answer: No. The learner can tell another trusted adult or the safeguarding lead and say that help is needed. A private opener could be: A learner feels afraid to say no and needs help to stay safe. They need not give details to peers. If danger is happening now, get staff help at once through the urgent safety procedure. A peer's role is to seek adult help, not investigate or fix the relationship.

hinge.question: In an invented story, one person keeps setting rules about who a friend may speak to. The friend feels afraid to say no. Which next step is safer?
options: A. Agree to half the rules so both people give something up.
B. Tell a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead and get help to stay safe.
C. Confront the person alone and demand an apology.
hinge.reason: Fear and rules that take away choice need adult help. The person does not have to negotiate control or confront someone alone. If danger is happening now, get staff help at once.
hinge.parallel_question: An invented friend accepts no and gives the other person space. Both feel safe. Could taking turns to listen help?
parallel_options: A. Yes, if both choose freely and can stop or ask for help.
B. Yes, but one person must give in to end every disagreement.
hinge.parallel_reason: Calm discussion is an option when both feel safe and have a real choice. Nobody has to give in, and either may pause or ask for adult help.

Supported: Use the model and word bank. In Case 1, point to safe choice or control. Finish: A pause is safe here because ___.
In Case 2, choose adult help or bargain about control. Point to the clue that helped. Finish: The person needs help because ___.
In Case 3, choose another trusted adult or the safeguarding lead. Point, say, draw or type one safe next step. Keep the model and usual aids.
Independent: Compare Cases 1 and 2. Find one detail showing free choice and one showing pressure or control. Explain why the next steps differ.
Write, type or arrange a short response for each case. Use calm listening only where both people feel safe. Add an adult help route for the unsafe case.
Use Case 3 to explain what could happen if the first adult is unavailable. Give a private help request and a safe next step. Keep the glossary and usual aids.
Aspire: Compare all three cases. Explain why the presence of choice and safety matters more than ending a disagreement quickly.
Explain why splitting the difference is a poor response to control in Case 2. Give a safer response without blaming or confronting the worried person.
Adapt the help plan in Case 3 if the first adult cannot listen. Distinguish urgent danger from a concern that still needs prompt adult support. Keep normal aids; no personal story is needed.

evidence_rows: Recognises safe disagreement and unsafe pressure
Uses a story detail about free choice, accepted limits, control or fear; avoids guessing from one emotion alone.
Chooses a response that fits safety
Calm listening or a pause only where both feel safe; adult help where control or fear is present; no forced compromise or confrontation.
Names a trusted adult and the safeguarding lead by role; chooses another adult if the first is unavailable; gets staff help at once for danger now.
misconceptions: Every relationship problem needs both people to compromise.
Safe disagreements may use shared problem-solving. Pressure, control or fear needs adult support and safety; a person need not give up a boundary to keep the peace.
If the first adult is busy, the learner must sort it out alone.
The learner can tell another trusted adult or the safeguarding lead. A peer can help them reach staff, but should not investigate, mediate an unsafe situation or promise secrecy.
teaching_points: A safe disagreement leaves each person free to say no, pause or seek help.
Calm listening may help when both people feel safe. A shared plan must be freely chosen.
Pressure, control or fear needs adult help. The person under pressure is not to blame.
Tell a trusted adult or the safeguarding lead. Try another trusted adult if needed. Get staff help at once if danger is happening now.
